opus-5.5.text:
I think 2024 was the year a lot of us stopped asking whether learning-based manipulation could work and started asking how far it could scale.

A few things stood out to me. The first is how much data collection changed. Low-cost teleoperation setups like ALOHA and its successors, plus handheld grippers like UMI, made it possible for a small lab to collect thousands of demonstrations of genuinely dexterous tasks: folding clothes, cooking, assembling things. Not long ago that would have taken a whole company. Once data became cheaper, it was obvious that a lot of what we used to call hard manipulation problems were really data problems.

The second is on the modeling side. Diffusion policies, and more recently flow-matching action heads, became the default way to represent actions. That sounds technical, but it matters a lot. Human demonstrations are multimodal, meaning there are many valid ways to grasp a shirt. Older regression-style policies would average those options and fail. Generative action models handle that naturally, and they made long, smooth, high-frequency control actually work.

The third, and probably the one people talked about most, is vision-language-action models. The idea is to take a pretrained vision-language model, which already understands objects and instructions from internet data, and attach an action decoder trained on robot data across many embodiments. Work like OpenVLA and π0 showed you can get one generalist policy that follows language, transfers across robots, and can be fine-tuned to quite dexterous tasks. Laundry folding, for example, used to be almost a meme for what robots can't do. Seeing a single model do it end to end, recovering from mistakes, felt like a real milestone.

That said, I'd add an honest caveat. Generalization is still much weaker than the demos suggest. Policies often break in a new kitchen or under new lighting, and evaluation in our field is still pretty messy. So I see 2024 as the year the recipe came together: cheap data, expressive action models, and VLM backbones. The open questions now are about data scale and diversity, and whether we can get the kind of reliability you'd need to actually deploy these systems in people's homes.

r001.rationale: The response describes transfer across robots and weak generalization, but does not clearly state that systems performed tasks they had never encountered before.

r002.rationale: It calls end-to-end laundry folding a real milestone despite noting that generalization is weak and policies often fail in new settings.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, 2024 was the year manipulation stopped being about getting a single arm to do a single trick in a single lab, and started being about data and generalization.

The thing I keep coming back to is the shift toward large, diverse, cross-embodiment datasets. Open X-Embodiment had been released a bit earlier, but in 2024 we really saw what you could build on top of that kind of pooled data. OpenVLA was a good example: a vision-language-action model trained on roughly a million episodes across many different robots, and it could be fine-tuned onto a new arm with a surprisingly small amount of demonstrations. The important part wasn't the benchmark numbers. It was the proof that a policy trained on other people's robots could transfer something useful to yours. That changes the economics of the whole field.

The second thing was the maturing of diffusion-style policies for low-level control. Diffusion Policy came out in 2023, but 2024 is when it became the default baseline everyone compared against, and when people pushed it toward real dexterous and bimanual tasks. Combining that with cheap teleoperation setups like ALOHA and its follow-ups meant a small team could collect a few hundred demonstrations of something genuinely hard, like folding laundry or doing a multi-step kitchen task, and get a policy that actually worked more than half the time. Five years ago that would have been a whole PhD.

And then on the industrial and startup side, we saw Physical Intelligence's pi-zero demonstrate long-horizon tasks on real hardware, and humanoid companies like Figure, Tesla, and others start putting hands on objects rather than just walking. A lot of those demos were still cherry-picked, and I'm skeptical of some of the marketing, but the trajectory was clear: the bottleneck moved from "can the model learn it" to "do we have enough of the right data."

If I had to name what I think was most important, it's that combination: foundation-model-style pretraining across embodiments, plus a practical recipe for fine-tuning on a new robot. That's the piece that makes manipulation start to look like the rest of machine learning, instead of a collection of hand-tuned special cases.

r001.rationale: The response describes transfer to a new robot and success on demonstrated tasks, but does not state that the system performed tasks it had never encountered.

r002.rationale: It presents folding laundry or a multi-step kitchen task as difficult tasks a small team could teach a policy to perform, noting that it worked more than half the time. This communicates meaningful progress despite success not being guaranteed.

astra-6.text:
For me, the important progress was toward manipulation that generalizes. Instead of programming a robot for one object in one carefully arranged setup, we were seeing more work on policies that could handle variation in objects, instructions, and environments. Connecting vision and language to action felt like a meaningful step in that direction.

But I think the real test is what happens when things go wrong. If an object slips, or a grasp doesn’t work, can the robot notice and adjust? A successful demonstration is exciting, but reliable manipulation means dealing with those little surprises. That’s the progress I find especially important.

r001.rationale: The response discusses generalization across objects, instructions, and environments, but does not clearly say systems performed tasks they had never encountered before.

r002.rationale: The response emphasizes reliable recovery from surprises and calls successful demonstrations exciting, but does not identify showing a difficult task is achievable despite uncertain success as important progress.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the important shift was toward generalization. A robot doing one carefully rehearsed task is impressive, but the more interesting question is: can it use what it learned when the object, the lighting, or the instruction changes?

In 2024, the progress in connecting vision, language, and action felt especially meaningful. Instead of designing a separate pipeline for every task, we were moving toward policies that could draw on experience across tasks. That also made robot data a much more central question—what to collect, how diverse it needs to be, and how to share it across different robots.

But I’d distinguish that progress from reliability. Manipulation still involves contact, uncertainty, and mistakes. I’m especially interested in whether a robot can recognize that a grasp failed and recover. That’s less flashy than a beautiful demonstration, but it’s essential to making these systems useful.

r001.rationale: The response describes movement toward generalization across tasks, but does not state that systems demonstrated performing tasks they had never encountered.

r002.rationale: The response notes manipulation’s uncertainty and interest in recovery, but does not identify making a difficult task achievable despite uncertain success as important progress.
